descript.abstract:
LANDFIRE’s Final Annual Disturbance 2025 (Dist25) product provides a comprehensive spatial and temporal record of landscape change occurring between October 1 and September 30 each year. As the third and final installment in the annual disturbance product suite, Dist25 delivers the finalized, quality-assured version for this release cycle.
The product captures landscape changes across varying scales including; 1) Satellite-Detected Change which captures natural or human-caused changes exceeding a 4.5hectare (11 acre) threshold and 2) Agency and Fire Program Data which incorporates reported fire activity and field treatments as small as 80 square meters.
Dist25 leverages three primary data streams, which are reviewed and refined by image analysts to maintain quality standards: 1) Data from national fire mapping programs, including fire severity and extent data from the most current Monitoring Trends in Burn Severity (MTBS), Burned Area Reflectance Classification (BARC), and Rapid Assessment of Vegetation Condition after Wildfire (RAVG). 2) Agency-reported events integrate 19 classes of disturbance and management treatment events (e.g., insects, disease, development, harvest, prescribed fire) contributed by various federal, state, and non-profit organizations (including NatureServe and The Nature Conservancy (TNC)). LANDFIRE standardizes these diverse source datasets into a unified schema within the LANDFIRE Disturbance and Treatment Polygons (Events) Geodatabase (GDB). 3) Satellite imagery from NASA/USGS Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) scenes are used to capture a significant volume of valuable landscape changes omitted by other reporting sources, particularly across private and non-government lands. Furthermore, this satellite-detected change data serves as the foundational source for assigning disturbance severity to all records across the entire product suite, with the sole exception of events mapped directly by national fire programs.
To mitigate data gaps, cloud cover, and seasonal anomalies, individual HLS scenes are stacked and composited band-by-band using the 15th, 50th, and 90th percentiles. Automated change detection is driven by the Multi-Index Integrated Change Algorithm (MIICA; Jin et al. 2013), the Delta Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (dNDVI), the Delta Normalized Burn Ratio (dNBR), and the Spatially Adaptable Filter for Error Reduction (SAFER) algorithm, [ES3.1] which utilizes composite imagery spanning the current and prior two years. Image analysts manually evaluate these outputs to differentiate true landscape change from phenological variations, image artifacts, or complex mapping environments like wetlands.
Cloud or water-induced data gaps within MTBS, BARC, or RAVG footprints are filled using predictive models trained on pre- and post-fire HLS data to ensure continuous severity and extent coverage.
Fires that fall below national program size thresholds are flagged as "fire-possible" if they intersect with Landsat 8 and 9 Burned Area (BA) Level 3 science products. Note that BA data integration is restricted to the Conterminous United States (CONUS).
Dist25 enforces a hierarchical priority ruleset to assign disturbance causality, timing, and severity. The Priority Hierarchy assures that attributes are assigned first from national fire mapping programs, second from the LANDFIRE Events GDB, and lastly from satellite-detected change imagery.
Severity values are mapped directly from fire program data when available. For user-contributed events and standalone satellite-detected changes, severity is modeled from the standard deviation of pre- and post-disturbance dNBR data, provided it coincides with a satellite-detected change footprint. If no satellite-based change is detected, the record is attributed as No Severity. This classification is common among management treatments (e.g. prescribed fire and chemical applications) and specific disturbance classes (e.g. insect and disease) where the landscape impact may not trigger automated spectral change thresholds.
Temporal assignments follow distinct rules based on the data source. For wildland fires the recorded start date is used to determine fiscal and calendar year assignments for national fire program data and for agency-submitted events specifically labeled as Wildland Fire or Wildland Fire Use. For treatments and other Events prescribed fires and all other agency-submitted event types use the provided end date for temporal assignments. Finally, for standalone satellite-detected disturbances, they are assigned to the fiscal year that aligns with the specific HLS composite imagery footprint in which the change was captured.
Dist25 represents the definitive version for the applicable mapping cycle. It differentiates from the preceding PDist product through a finalized go-back review process. During this final phase, LANDFIRE staff incorporate late-arriving agency event data, management treatments, or national fire program records submitted after the initial data call deadline. Users requiring the most complete and quality-assured record of landscape change should utilize the final Dist product.
descript.purpose:
The LANDFIRE 2025 Update (LF 2025, version 2.6.0) is the sixth update to the LF 2016 Remap base map (version 2.0.0) and will be releasing throughout calendar year 2026.
LF 2025 products are designed to facilitate national and regional level strategic fire and resource management planning and reporting of management activities. The principal purposes of the products include providing: 1) national level landscape scale geospatial products to support fire and fuels management planning and 2) consistent fuels products to support fire planning, analysis, and budgeting to evaluate fire management alternatives.
Products are created at a 30meter raster; however, the applicability of products varies by location and specific use. LF products were designed to support 1) national (all states) strategic planning, 2) regional (single large states or groups of smaller states), and 3) strategic/tactical planning for large sub regional landscapes and Fire Management Units (FMUs) (such as significant portions of states or multiple federal administrative entities). The applicability of LF products to support fire and land management planning on smaller areas will vary by product, location, and specific use. Managers and planners must evaluate LF products according to the scale and requirements specific to their needs.

procstep.procdesc:
Beginning with the new base map of LANDFIRE 2016 Remap (LF Remap), LF products were created using recent advances in image compositing, tiling algorithms, and faster computing hardware to ensure that LF products remained relevant. LF Remap leveraged the Landsat archive, lidar data, and user contributed field plot data compiled into the LF Reference Database (LFRDB), to create new vegetation products.
Reference resources utilized in LF Remap and all updates since includes but is not limited to: Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) program plot data, Landsat Dynamic Surface Water Extent (DSWE), the National Land Cover Database (NLCD), and National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS).

For LF 2025 reference resources include but are not limited to: Monitoring Trends in Burn Severity (MTBS), Burned Area Reflectance Classification (BARC) and Rapid Assessment of Vegetation Condition after Wildfire (RAVG). Then the Protected Areas Database of the United States (PAD) was used to remove agriculture on non-irrigated federal and state protected lands. A rasterized version of the Microsoft building footprint and Wildfire Risk to Communities (WRC) was used to update developed areas. Two main submitted sources were also used: the US Bureau of Land Management (BLM) and National Park Service (NPS).

Disturbances in LF 2025 were also identified with LF's Remote Sensing of Landscape Change (RSLC), which identifies spectral change in vegetation using automated algorithms and image analyst review of the entire country with Landsat imagery. Burned Area (BA) data from Landsat was also used and national events (polygons) were used to identify areas and types of disturbance.
To read more about LF reference resources go to https://landfire.gov/reference. Information about LF product testing is available by request or via the website at https://www.landfire.gov.
